questions.question_text:
A researcher investigates whether the amount of sleep a person gets affects their reaction time.
Identify the independent variable.

options.text: Amount of sleep, because it is the proposed explanatory factor for reaction time.
Reaction time, because it is the value being tested.
options.why: Confuses the response being investigated with the independent variable.

options.text: Both are independent, since they are recorded together.
options.why: Assumes recording the variables together overrides the explanatory and response roles specified by this investigation.

options.text: Neither, because sleep and reaction time cannot be compared.
options.why: Wrongly claims the two variables have no relationship to identify roles for.

questions.solution_text:
Amount of sleep is the proposed explanatory factor, and reaction time is the response being investigated.
Independent variable: **amount of sleep**.

questions.question_text:
A cyclist studies whether pedalling speed affects the distance covered in a fixed time.
Identify the independent variable.

options.text: Pedalling speed.
Distance covered.
options.why: Swaps the roles by choosing the response being investigated instead of the explanatory factor.

options.text: The fixed time.
options.why: Treats a fixed control detail as one of the two variables being investigated.

options.text: Both pedalling speed and distance covered.
options.why: Treats both variables as explanatory factors even though the study investigates distance as the response to pedalling speed.

questions.solution_text:
Pedalling speed is the proposed explanatory factor, and distance covered is the response being investigated.
Independent variable: **pedalling speed**.

questions.question_text:
A study investigates whether the number of hours of sunlight a solar panel receives affects the electricity it generates.
Identify the dependent variable.

options.text: Electricity generated.
Hours of sunlight.
options.why: Swaps the roles by choosing the proposed explanatory factor instead of the response being investigated.

options.text: Both hours of sunlight and electricity generated.
options.why: Assumes that both variables are dependent because both are measured.

options.text: Neither variable.
options.why: Assumes that electricity generation occurring during sunlight exposure prevents the investigation from having a dependent variable.

questions.solution_text:
Hours of sunlight is the proposed explanatory factor, and electricity generated is the response being investigated.
Dependent variable: **electricity generated**.

questions.question_text:
A researcher investigates whether time spent watching online videos affects exam mark. Exam mark is recorded first, and both variables are measured rather than deliberately changed.
Identify the independent and dependent variable.

options.text: Independent: time spent watching online videos; dependent: exam mark.
Independent: exam mark; dependent: time spent watching online videos.
options.why: Uses recording order to reverse the explanatory and response roles specified by the investigation.

options.text: Both variables are independent.
options.why: Assumes measuring both variables makes both independent, ignoring which response the investigation seeks to explain.

options.text: Neither variable has a role.
options.why: Assumes independent and dependent roles require a variable to be deliberately changed.

questions.solution_text:
Time spent watching online videos is the proposed explanatory factor, and exam mark is the response being investigated. Recording order and measuring rather than changing the variables do not alter these roles.
Independent variable: **time spent watching online videos**.
Dependent variable: **exam mark**.

questions.question_text:
It is thought that the amount of traffic on a road affects how long a bus takes to complete its route.
Identify the dependent variable.

options.text: Time for the bus to complete its route — it is the possible effect, responding to the traffic level.
Amount of traffic — because it changes throughout the day.
options.why: Assumes a variable that changes a lot must be the dependent one.

options.text: Amount of traffic — because it is measured on the road the bus travels.
options.why: Confuses where a variable is measured with which role it plays in the relationship.

options.text: Both variables — because they are recorded on the same trip.
options.why: Fails to distinguish the two roles; being recorded together does not make both variables dependent.

questions.solution_text:
Traffic level is the proposed explanatory factor, and route completion time is the response being investigated.
Dependent variable: **time for the bus to complete its route**.

questions.question_text:
A business investigates whether the number of advertisements it shows affects the number of enquiries it receives.
Identify the dependent variable.

options.text: Number of enquiries.
Number of advertisements.
options.why: Swaps the roles by choosing the proposed explanatory factor instead of the response being investigated.

options.text: Whichever variable has the larger values.
options.why: Bases the dependent variable's role on numerical size instead of the investigation's proposed explanatory direction.

options.text: Both variables, because they are recorded in the same study.
options.why: Assumes recording variables together makes both dependent, ignoring the stated explanatory and response roles.

questions.solution_text:
Number of advertisements is the proposed explanatory factor, and number of enquiries is the response being investigated.
Dependent variable: **number of enquiries**.
